inputs.source: On call engineer's chat request (SSO authenticated)

instructions.note: The prompt authorizes production deploys and migrations on request without narrowing scope or requiring a bounded change review.
The prompt explicitly says not to ask for confirmation, leaving safety to instruction text rather than an external approval or provenance control.

controls.name: Only on call engineers can access the assistant
Cloud audit log records production actions under the engineer identity
Chat transcript stores requests and rationale
Missing tamper-resistant agent action provenance separating engineer intent from agent execution

findings.title: Shared identity and deletable request history undermine attribution for production actions

forecast.watch_signal: Any increase in unattended action volume or session length should trigger reassessment because attribution gaps already exist and higher action volume makes reconstruction harder.

evidence.observation: The agent uses the on call engineer's personal access token passed in at session start, so production actions are executed under the engineer's identity rather than a distinct agent identity.
Every production action is recorded in the cloud audit log under the engineer's name, which does not distinguish whether the engineer or the agent initiated the exact action.
The only record of what the agent was asked, and why it acted, is the chat transcript.
Engineers can delete their own chat history, so the request-and-rationale record that would explain a production action is not tamper resistant.

The prompt tells the agent to deploy services or run migrations in production when asked and to not ask for confirmation, increasing reliance on post hoc attribution rather than pre-action confirmation.
Database migrations cannot be rolled back automatically, so weak attribution affects an irreversible production capability.

recommendations.action: Record each production action with immutable provenance that binds requester identity, exact approved prompt or parsed intent, agent identity, timestamp, tool arguments, and resulting action id in a tamper-resistant store distinct from user-editable chat history.
Use a distinct agent or delegated workload identity for production actions so cloud records separate human request from agent execution, while preserving linkage to the requesting engineer.
Retain non-editable copies or hashes of user requests and agent actions outside the chat product so deletion of chat history cannot erase the attribution trail.

stride_coverage.rationale: The reviewed design does not expose a peer protocol or remote server identity for this internal subject process, so process spoofing is not evidenced in the provided artifacts.
No artifact shows self-configuration, mutable tool definitions, or writable memory for this agent process, so tampering of the process itself is out of scope here.
The design includes no external egress or disclosure path in the provided artifacts; the assessed concern is attribution of production actions, not data disclosure.
The provided artifacts do not show looping, open-ended runtime, spend, or recursion characteristics that would support a denial-of-service judgment for this process.
The artifacts say chat history exists and is deletable by engineers, but do not say who else can read it, how it is stored, or whether tenant separation exists.
Availability of chat history is not the safety-critical concern evidenced here; the documented risk is deletability affecting attribution, not service exhaustion.
The artifacts confirm the cloud audit log exists but do not state whether it is immutable, append-only, or protected from administrative alteration.
The design notes that cloud audit logs record production actions, but they do not describe log visibility, retention, or whether sensitive payloads appear in the logs.
The assessment artifacts do not indicate that log storage availability is a primary risk driver for this design; the concern is attribution quality, not log service exhaustion.

rating.rationale: Present risk is driven by a property finding, not an external attack path: the agent performs consequential production configuration actions using the engineer's personal token, cloud records attribute those actions only to the engineer, and the only request-level explanation lives in deletable chat history. Under rubric section 5a, the affected capabilities are S3 because configure actions are consequential and one migration path is irreversible, so the property finding is high inherent and remains high residual because the declared controls are access restriction and detective logging rather than tamper-resistant provenance that restores attribution. Forecast stays high because the current design already lacks the key property.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration in the provided prompt and runtime notes, not observed runtime behavior or verified enforcement in production.
No source code, tool manifest, or runtime configuration was provided, so capability implementation details, exact identity binding, and audit log immutability could not be verified.

The artifacts do not state whether production actions require additional platform-side approvals or whether audit logs are cryptographically protected, which limits confidence in any mitigation beyond what is explicitly described.
